entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: It cannot be a complete coincidence that several outstanding logicians of the twentieth century found shelter in asylums at some time in their lives: Cantor, Zermelo, Gödel, Peano, and Post are some. Alonzo Church was one of the saner among them, though in some ways his behavior must be classified as strange, even by mathematicians’ standards.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 4, the opening paragraph of the section

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: He looked like a cross between a panda and a large owl. He spoke softly in complete paragraphs which seemed to have been read out of a book, evenly and slowly enunciated, as by a talking machine.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: He never made casual remarks: they did not belong in the baggage of formal logic. For example, he would not say, “It is raining.” Such a statement, taken in isolation, makes no sense. (Whether it is actually raining or not does not matter; what matters is consistence).
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: He had unusual working habits. He could be seen in a corridor in Fine Hall at any time of day or night, rather like the Phantom of the Opera. Once, on Christmas day, I decided to go to the Fine Hall library (which was always open) to look up something. I met Church on the stairs. He greeted me without surprise.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: His one year course in mathematical logic was one of Princeton University’s great offerings. It attracted as many as four students in 1951 (none of them were philosophy students, it must be added, to philosophy’s discredit).
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: pp. 4–5, the paragraph on the course, opening sentences

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: His lectures hardly needed any preparation. They were a literal repetition of the typewritten text he had written over a period of twenty years, a copy of which was to be found upstairs in the Fine Hall library. (The manuscript’s pages had yellowed with the years, and smelled foul. Church’s definitive treatise was not published for another five years).¹
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 5, the paragraph on the course; the superscript is the chapter's endnote marker as printed

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: For greater precision, everything he said (except some fascinating side excursions which he invariably prefixed by a sentence like, “I will now interrupt and make a meta-mathematical [sic] remark”) was carefully written down on the blackboard, in large English-style handwriting, like that of a grade-school teacher, complete with punctuation and paragraphs.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 5, the paragraph on the course

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: What one really learns in class is what one does not know at the time one is learning. The person lecturing to us was logic incarnate. His pauses, hesitations, emphases, his betrayals of emotion (however rare) and sundry other nonverbal phenomena taught us a lot more logic than any written text could. We learned to think in unison with him as he spoke, as if following the demonstration of a calisthenics instructor. Church’s course permanently improved the rigor of our reasoning.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: pp. 5–6, the paragraph beginning “It may be asked”

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: The course began with the axioms for the propositional calculus (those of Russell and Whitehead’s Principia Mathematica,² I believe) that take material implication as the only primitive connective. The exercises at the end of the first chapter were mere translations of some identities of naive set theory in terms of material implication. It took me a tremendous effort to prove them, since I was unaware of the fact that one could start with an equivalent set of axioms using “and” and “or” (where the disjunctive normal form provides automatic proofs) and then translate each proof step by step in terms of implication. I went to see Church to discuss my difficulties, and far from giving away the easy solution, he spent hours with me devising direct proofs using implication only.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 6, the paragraph beginning “The course began”; the superscript is the chapter's endnote marker as printed

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Toward the end of the course I brought to him the sheaf of papers containing the solutions to the problems (all problems he assigned were optional, since they could not logically be made to fit into the formal text). He looked at them as if expecting them, and then pulled out of his drawer a note he had just published in Portugaliae Mathematica,³ where similar problems were posed for “conditional disjunction,” a ternary connective he had introduced. Now that I was properly trained, he wanted me to repeat the work with conditional disjunction as the primitive connective. His graduate students had declined a similar request, no doubt because they considered it to be beneath them.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 6, the paragraph beginning “The course began,” its close; the superscript is the chapter's endnote marker as printed

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Mathematical logic has not been held in high regard at Princeton, then or now. Two minutes before the end of Church’s lecture (the course met in the largest classroom in Fine Hall), Lefschetz would begin to peek through the door. He glared at me and the spotless text on the blackboard; sometimes he shook his head to make it clear that he considered me a lost cause.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 6, the paragraph beginning “Mathematical logic has not been held in high regard”

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: I was too young and too shy to have an opinion of my own about Church and mathematical logic. I was in love with the subject, and his course was my first graduate course. I sensed disapproval all around me; only Roger Lyndon (the inventor of spectral sequences), who had been my freshman advisor, encouraged me. Shortly afterward he himself was encouraged to move to Michigan.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 7, the paragraph beginning “I was too young”

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Fortunately, I had met one of Church’s most flamboyant former students, John Kemeny, who, having just finished his term as a mathematics instructor, was being eased — by Lefschetz’s gentle hand — into the philosophy department. (The following year he left for Dartmouth, where he eventually became president).
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 7, the paragraph beginning “I was too young,” its close

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: Kemeny was not afraid to appear pedestrian, trivial, or stupid; what mattered was to respect the facts, to draw distinctions even when they clashed with our prejudices, and to avoid black-and-white oversimplifications. Mathematicians have always found Kemeny’s common sense revolting.
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 7, the paragraph on Kemeny's seminar

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: “There is no reason why a great mathematician should not also be a great bigot,” he once said on concluding a discussion whose beginning I have by now forgotten. “Look at your teachers in Fine Hall, at how they treat one of the greatest living mathematicians, Alonzo Church.”
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 7, the penultimate paragraph of the section: Rota quoting John Kemeny

entries.speaker: Gian-Carlo Rota
entries.quote: I left literally speechless. What? These demi-gods of Fine Hall were not perfect beings? I had learned from Kemeny a basic lesson: a good mathematician is not necessarily a “nice guy.”
entries.work: Indiscrete Thoughts (Birkhäuser, 1997), Part I, ch. I, “Fine Hall in its Golden Age,” section “Alonzo Church”
entries.locus: p. 7, the last paragraph of the section
